🚨 Malicious iPhone Ads Hunt Crypto Seed Phrases in 47 Countries

Security firm Confiant has traced over 480 malicious ad domains operating across more than 47 countries — all targeting iPhone users with attacks designed to steal crypto wallet recovery phrases and personal data.

Seed phrases are the skeleton key to any crypto wallet. Lose one to attackers and your funds are gone, no recourse. The attack surface here — legitimate-looking ads on iPhones — is exactly the kind of vector most users aren't watching for.

Hardware wallets and extreme caution around any prompt asking for recovery phrases remain the obvious countermeasures.

📌 Deepfake Giveaways: Why No One Will Ever Double Your Crypto

Main Points
⏺ Scammers now use AI deepfakes of famous people on fake livestreams
⏺ The pitch is always the same: send crypto, get double back
⏺ This post explains how the trick works and the one rule that beats it



1️⃣ Core Idea — A "giveaway" that asks you to send money first is not a giveaway. It is a one-way transfer to a stranger's wallet.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — AI can now copy a famous face and voice convincingly. A hijacked channel with a real-looking stream makes it feel official.
3️⃣ Example — This week a fake Tesla stream with a deepfake Elon Musk drew over 500,000 viewers. Coinbase says its AI blocked about $4.7 million that customers tried to send.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — YouTube and X livestreams, QR codes on screen, "limited time" countdowns and fake comment sections full of "I got paid!"
5️⃣ Practical Rule — If anyone promises to send back more crypto than you send, it is a scam. Every time. Close the stream and report it.
Final Thoughts

A crypto transfer can't be undone. No celebrity, exchange or project needs your coins to "verify" a giveaway — real airdrops never ask you to pay first.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
